井陘男 uses the rank 男 (baron), not 侯 (marquis).
Awarded five hundred bolts of silk, he distributed them among his friends within days, winning praise throughout the realm.
Awarded five hundred bolts of silk, he distributed them among his friends within days, and the people of his time praised him.
時人稱之 means people of the time praised him; "throughout the realm" is not in the source.
He served successively as prefect of Wudou and Hanyang, winning renown for integrity in both posts.
He served successively as prefect of Wudu and Hanyang, winning renown for integrity in both posts.
武都 is romanized Wudu; "Wudou" misrenders the commandery name.
He served successively as Administrator of Wudou and Hanyang, both offices famed for integrity.
He served successively as Administrator of Wudu and Hanyang, both offices famed for integrity.
武都 is romanized Wudu; "Wudou" misrenders the commandery name.
During Tianping he was posthumously enfeoffed as governor of Ding province.
During Tianping he was posthumously granted the title of governor of Ding province.
贈定州刺史 is a posthumous grant of an office title; 刺史 is not a fief, so "enfeoffed" is wrong.
In the Tianping period he was posthumously enfeoffed as Governor of Ding Province.
In the Tianping period he was posthumously granted the title Governor of Ding Province.
贈定州刺史 is a posthumous grant of an office title; 刺史 is not a fief, so "enfeoffed" is wrong.
Early in Putai, Yuan petitioned to use his own rank to secure posthumous honors for his father; the court enfeoffed his father posthumously as governor of Ping province.
Early in Putai, Yuan petitioned to use his own rank to secure posthumous honors for his father; the court granted his father the posthumous title of governor of Ping province.
詔贈平州刺史 is a posthumous grant of an office title; 刺史 is not a fief, so "enfeoffed" is wrong.
In the early Putai period Yuan petitioned to use his own rank to request posthumous honors for his father; an edict enfeoffed the father posthumously as Governor of Ping Province.
In the early Putai period Yuan petitioned to use his own rank to request posthumous honors for his father; an edict posthumously granted the father the title Governor of Ping Province.
詔贈平州刺史 is a posthumous grant of an office title, not an enfeoffment.
He later served as a doctor of the grand imperial sacrifices, accepted office from Prince Yuan of Taiyuan Erzhu Rong, and Rong kept him as left aide on the northern expedition grand commission.

He later concurrently served as an erudite of the Chamberlain for Ceremonials, accepted office from Erzhu Rong, Prince of Taiyuan, and Rong kept him as left assistant of the Grand Branch Department for the Northern Circuit.
太原王爾硃榮 is "Erzhu Rong, Prince of Taiyuan"; there is no "Prince Yuan". 兼 means concurrently, and 北道大行臺 is the grand branch department of the northern circuit, not an expedition commission.

Later he also served as a doctor of the Grand Imperial Sacrifices, received appointment from Prince Yuan of Taiyuan Erzhu Rong, and Rong retained him as left aide of the Northern Expedition Grand Commission.

Later he also concurrently served as an erudite of the Chamberlain for Ceremonials, received appointment from Erzhu Rong, Prince of Taiyuan, and Rong retained him as Left Assistant of the Grand Branch Department for the Northern Circuit.
太原王 is Erzhu Rong's title Prince of Taiyuan; "Prince Yuan of Taiyuan" invents a name. 北道大行臺左丞 is Left Assistant of the Northern Circuit Grand Branch Department.
At the libation ceremony opening the lectures, Yuan joined Wen Zisheng, Wei Jijing, and Li Yexing in composing extemporaneous verses.
At the libation ceremony opening the lectures, Yuan, together with Wen Zisheng, Wei Jijing, and Li Yexing, served as the questioners who picked out passages for discussion.
擿句 (摘句) in a lecture setting means selecting passages to pose questions to the lecturer; nothing is said about composing verses.
At the libation and opening of lectures, Yuan together with Wen Zisheng, Wei Jijing, and Li Yexing all composed extemporaneous verses.
At the libation and opening of lectures, Yuan together with Wen Zisheng, Wei Jijing, and Li Yexing all served as passage-pickers (questioners).
擿句 means picking out passages (to raise questions) at the lecture, not composing verses.
The emperor referred the matter to the Ministry of Works.
The emperor referred the matter to the Department of State Affairs.
詔付尚書 sends the matter to the 尚書 (Department of State Affairs); "Ministry of Works" (工部) is a mistranslation.
An edict was sent to the Ministry of Works.
An edict referred it to the Department of State Affairs.
尚書 here is the Department of State Affairs, not the Ministry of Works.
Though his rank was eminent, he remained as poor as ever; his integrity was valued throughout the realm.
Though his rank was eminent, he remained as poor as ever; his integrity was valued by his contemporaries.
為時所重 means he was esteemed by the people of his time; "throughout the realm" overstates the source.
Posthumously enfeoffed as minister of the imperial stud and governor of Ji province, with the posthumous title Ming.
He was posthumously granted the titles of minister of the imperial stud and governor of Ji province, with the posthumous name Ming.
贈太僕卿、濟州刺史 is a posthumous grant of office titles, not an enfeoffment; the sentence also lacks a subject.
Posthumously enfeoffed as Minister of the Imperial Stud and Governor of Ji Province, posthumous title Ming.
Posthumously granted the titles Minister of the Imperial Stud and Governor of Ji Province, posthumous title Ming.
贈 grants office titles posthumously; it is not an enfeoffment.
Early in Wuding he was posthumously enfeoffed as grand general of the guard, minister of the court for state affairs, and governor of Ying province, with the posthumous title Yi.
Early in Wuding he was posthumously granted the titles of grand general of the guard, minister of capital officials, and governor of Ying province, with the posthumous title Yi.
贈 is a posthumous grant of office titles, not an enfeoffment; 都官尚書 is the Minister of Capital Officials, not a "minister of the court for state affairs".
In the early Wuding period posthumously enfeoffed as Grand General of the Guard, Minister of the Court for State Affairs, and Governor of Ying Province, posthumous title Yi.
In the early Wuding period posthumously granted the titles Grand General of the Guard, Minister of Capital Officials, and Governor of Ying Province, posthumous title Yi.
贈 grants titles posthumously; 都官尚書 is Minister of Capital Officials.
Zhang Hua, original name Guoman, was a native of Dai commandery.
Zhang Huayuan, courtesy name Guoman, was a native of Dai commandery.
The name is 張華原 (as in the chapter lists and s0147 ff.) with courtesy name 國滿; the displaced comma in 張華，原字國滿 led to the false reading "Zhang Hua, original name Guoman".
Zhang Hua, original name Guoman, was a man of Dai Commandery.
Zhang Huayuan, styled Guoman, was a man of Dai Commandery.
The name is 張華原 with courtesy name (字) 國滿; "original name" results from mis-segmenting 張華原字國滿.
He first served as legal affairs officer in Shenwu's rapid cavalry headquarters, was enfeoffed as baron of Xincheng, and rose repeatedly on the great chancellor's staff.
He first served as legal affairs officer in Shenwu's rapid cavalry headquarters, was granted the rank of Earl of Xincheng, and rose repeatedly on the great chancellor's staff.
新城伯 is an earldom (伯), not a barony (男).
At first he served as legal affairs officer in Shenwu's Rapid Cavalry headquarters, enfeoffed as Baron of Xincheng, and was promoted repeatedly to staff of the great chancellor's office.
At first he served as legal affairs officer in Shenwu's Rapid Cavalry headquarters, enfeoffed as Earl of Xincheng, and was promoted repeatedly to staff of the great chancellor's office.
新城伯 uses the rank 伯 (earl), not 男 (baron).
Posthumously enfeoffed as duke of the ministry of works and left vice minister of the imperial secretariat.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Minister of Works and Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

司空公 is the Minister of Works (one of the Three Excellencies), not a "duke of the ministry"; 尚書左僕射 is Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs; 贈 is a posthumous grant, not an enfeoffment.
Posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of the Ministry of Works and Left Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Posthumously granted the titles Minister of Works and Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
司空公 is the Excellency Minister of Works; 尚書左僕射 is Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs; 贈 is not an enfeoffment.
Shao then jested: "You court famous men."
Shao then jested with Ye: "You are just courting a reputation."
卿邀名人也 means "you are a man who seeks fame" (邀名 = court a reputation), not "you court famous men".
Shao then jested with Ye: "You invite famous men."
Shao then jested with Ye: "You are a man who seeks fame."
邀名人 is 邀名 + 人: "a person who courts fame", not "invite famous men".
Within ten days Shao's attendants Wang Side and Dong Weijin both used the horse meat as a pretext; chief administrator Pei Yingqi secretly memorialized against Ye.
Within ten days Shao's attendants Wang Side and Dong Weijin both used the horse's death as a pretext to ask for meat, and chief administrator Pei Yingqi secretly reported them.
為長史裴英起密啟 is passive: the attendants were secretly reported by Pei Yingqi; the source does not say he memorialized against Meng Ye.
He also ordered officials' memorials reviewed for improprieties; the emperor had men strike Ye's head with a horsewhip until he bled.
He was also ordered to inspect the officials, and when his report was improper the emperor had men strike Ye's head with a horsewhip until he bled.
又令點檢百官，敷奏失所: Meng Ye was ordered to inspect the officials and his report was improper; the translation loses who was ordered and why he was beaten.
He arranged his son's marriage with the imperial in-law Tuo clan.
He arranged his son's marriage with the Zhaluo clan, intimates of the court.
吒羅 is romanized Zhaluo (吒 = zhà); "Tuo" misreads the clan name.
When arranging his son's marriage, it was with the imperial in-law Tuo clan.
When arranging his son's marriage, it was with the Zhaluo clan, intimates of the court.
吒羅氏 is the Zhaluo clan; "Tuo" misreads 吒.
His son, a staff officer in Prince Xiaoxian of Pingyuan's chancellor's office, had fashionable brocade jackets and silk trousers made.
His son, who through hereditary privilege became an acting adjutant in the chancellor's office of Duan Xiaoxian, Prince of Pingyuan, had fashionable brocade jackets and silk trousers made.
平原王段孝先 is Duan Xiaoxian, Prince of Pingyuan, not "Prince Xiaoxian"; 以廕 (hereditary privilege) and 行 (acting) are omitted.
His son, ennobled as staff officer in the chancellor's office of Prince Xiaoxian of Pingyuan, Duan Xiaoxian, had contemporary fashionable brocade jackets and silk trousers made.
His son, through hereditary privilege, became acting adjutant in the chancellor's office of Duan Xiaoxian, Prince of Pingyuan, and had contemporary fashionable brocade jackets and silk trousers made.
平原王段孝先 is Duan Xiaoxian, Prince of Pingyuan; "Prince Xiaoxian of Pingyuan, Duan Xiaoxian" duplicates and misreads the title; 以廕 means by hereditary privilege, not "ennobled".
The Tuo family flaunted the marriage connection with boastful display.
The Zhaluo family flaunted the marriage connection with boastful display.
吒羅 is the Zhaluo clan; "Tuo" misreads 吒.
The Tuo family again relied on the marriage tie, showing off and boasting.
The Zhaluo family again relied on the marriage tie, showing off and boasting.
吒羅 is the Zhaluo clan; "Tuo" misreads 吒.
His father Bei served Wei as vice minister of the imperial clan.
His father Bei served Wei, rising to vice minister of the guards.
衛尉少卿 is Vice Minister of the Guards (Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison), not of the imperial clan (宗正).
His father Bei served Wei as far as Vice Minister of the Imperial Clan.
His father Bei served Wei as far as Vice Minister of the Guards.
衛尉少卿 is Vice Minister of the Guards, not of the Imperial Clan.
Qi Wenxiang, as palace guard of the fifth order, opened a staff and made him penal-affairs officer, often encouraging him.
Qi Wenxiang, who held the rank of yitong with his own headquarters, made him adjutant for penal affairs and often encouraged him.
儀同開府 is the rank "equal in dignity to the Three Excellencies" with an opened headquarters; "palace guard of the fifth order" is a mistranslation.
Qi Wenxiang, holding the rank of palace guard of the fifth order, opened a staff office and made him penal-affairs staff officer, often encouraging and commending him.
Qi Wenxiang, holding the rank of yitong with an opened headquarters, made him penal-affairs staff officer, often encouraging and commending him.
儀同開府 means holding yitong (equal to the Three Excellencies) rank with an opened headquarters, not "palace guard of the fifth order".
A rich Cheng clan in Yimo county, pressed by bandits, said: "My goods are with Lord Su"—and the bandits departed.
A very rich man surnamed Cheng of Yimo county in Ji province, hard pressed by bandits, said: "My goods are with Lord Su"—and the bandits departed.
成氏 here is a single speaker (he says 我物), a man surnamed Cheng, not a clan; 冀州 (Ji province) is omitted.
The Daoist Daoyan, monastic superintendent of Jizhou, was vastly wealthy and lent at interest, often having counties collect for him.
The monk Daoyan, Buddhist superintendent of Ji province, was vastly wealthy and lent at interest in the commandery, often having the commandery and counties collect for him.
In this period 道人 denotes a Buddhist monk, and 沙門統 is the Buddhist monastic superintendent; "Daoist" is wrong.
The Daoist Daoyan was monastic superintendent of Jizhou, with vast wealth, lending at interest in the commandery, often having the commandery and counties collect for him.
The monk (道人) Daoyan was Buddhist superintendent (沙門統) of Jizhou, with vast wealth, lending at interest in the commandery, often having the commandery and counties collect for him.
道人 here means a Buddhist monk, consistent with 沙門統; "Daoist" is wrong.
He hung them on the investigation beam and never cut them.
He hung them on a beam of his audience hall and never cut them.
査事 here stands for the audience hall (聽事/廳事) where he conducted business; "investigation beam" is not meaningful English.
Each spring he gathered great scholars to lecture at the commandery school and had clerks study in spare moments.
Each spring he gathered great Confucian scholars such as Wei Jilong and Tian Yuanfeng to lecture at the commandery school, and had the clerks study in moments spared from their documents.
The names 衛覬隆 and 田元鳳 are omitted from the idiomatic translation.
Each spring he gathered great Confucians Wei Kilong, Tian Yuanfeng, and others to lecture at the commandery school; in their spare time from documents he had all clerks study books.
Each spring he gathered great Confucians Wei Jilong, Tian Yuanfeng, and others to lecture at the commandery school; in their spare time from documents he had all clerks study books.
覬 is romanized ji; "Kilong" misspells 衛覬隆 (Wei Jilong).
Recalled as director of the imperial secretariat and rectifier of the minister of justice, courtiers sighed at his demotion; Xin Shu said: "Upright and correct—his name fits; he will surely succeed."
Recalled as court rectifier and rectifier of the Court of Justice, courtiers sighed that he was held back; Minister Xin Shu said: "Upright and correct—his name fits; he will surely succeed."
司直 is the court rectifier (a judicial-review post) and 廷尉正 the rectifier of the Court of Justice; "director of the imperial secretariat" is wrong, and 尚書 (Minister) is dropped.

Soon he was recalled as Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Minister of Justice rectifier; court gentlemen sighed at his demotion; Minister Xin Shu said: "Upright and correct—the name fixes the substance; no worry he will not succeed."

Soon he was recalled as Court Rectifier and Rectifier of the Court of Justice; court gentlemen sighed that he was held back; Minister Xin Shu said: "Upright and correct—the name fixes the substance; no worry he will not succeed."
司直 is Court Rectifier, not "Director of the Imperial Secretariat"; 廷尉正 is Rectifier of the Court of Justice.
Earlier as prefect of Qinghe, Pei Xianbo was governor of Jizhou.
Earlier, when Qiong was prefect of Qinghe, Pei Xianbo was governor of Jizhou.
The idiomatic line drops the subject 瓊 and makes Pei Xianbo the prefect of Qinghe.
Pei feared framing Qiong because of earlier words; Qiong reported his wrongful detention and discussants admired his fairness.
Pei, because of his earlier words, feared that Qiong would bring him down; instead Qiong spoke up for Pei's wrongful stagnation, and discussants admired his fairness.
恐為瓊陷 means Pei feared being brought down by Qiong, not that Pei feared framing Qiong; 申其枉滯 means Qiong spoke up for Pei's unjust lack of advancement.
Pei, because of the earlier words, feared framing Qiong; Qiong reported his wrongful detention and discussants admired his fairness.
Pei, because of the earlier words, feared being brought down by Qiong; Qiong reported his wrongful stagnation, and discussants admired his fairness.
恐為瓊陷 is passive: Pei feared being brought down by Qiong.
Temple and ministry case records began with Qiong.
The practice of the Court of Justice endorsing Censorate cases began with Qiong.
寺 here is a government court (the Court of Justice) and 台 the Censorate, not a temple; the line records a procedural innovation.
Temple and ministry case records began with Qiong.
The Court's endorsement of Censorate cases began with Qiong.
寺署台案: 寺 (the Court) signs (署) the Censorate's (台) cases; "Temple" mistranslates 寺.
That year Huainan had famine; he allowed grain purchases north of the Huai.
That year Huainan had famine; he petitioned to allow grain purchases north of the Huai.
啟聽 means he memorialized requesting permission; he did not himself allow it.
Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an below the capital were notoriously hard to govern; in chaotic times imperial kin pressed endless requests.
Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an, the three counties under the capital, lay beneath the imperial carriage and were long known as hard to govern.
The appended clause about chaotic times and imperial kin belongs to s0324 and is not in this line.
Near the capital lay Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an—three counties long hard to govern under the imperial hub; compounded by chaotic times and slack law, imperial kin made endless requests.
Near the capital lay Ye, Linzhang, and Cheng'an—three counties under the imperial hub, long known as hard to govern.
"compounded by chaotic times and slack law, imperial kin made endless requests" is not in this line (it renders s0324).
Law's net hung slack; meritorious ministers and imperial affines pressed requests from every side.
Moreover, in chaotic government and hard times the net of law was not upheld, and close ministers and palace affines pressed requests from every side.
近臣內戚 means close ministers and palace affines, not "meritorious ministers and imperial affines"; 政亂時艱 is omitted.
Compounded by chaotic government and hard times, the net of law was not established, and meritorious ministers and imperial affines made requests from every quarter.
Compounded by chaotic government and hard times, the net of law was not established, and close ministers and palace affines made requests from every quarter.
近臣 means close (intimate) ministers, not "meritorious ministers".
Later Qubing was implicated in Yuwen Jiong's affair.
Later Qubing was implicated in Yuchi Jiong's affair.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong; "Yuwen Jiong" misreads the surname 尉遲.
Later Qubing was implicated in Yuwen Jiong's affair.
Later Qubing was implicated in Yuchi Jiong's affair.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not Yuwen Jiong.
Liang Yanguang, styled Xiuzhi, was from Wushi in Anding.
Liang Yanguang, styled Xiuzhi, was from Wuzhi in Anding.
In the place name 烏氏 the character 氏 is read zhī (Wuzhi).
Liang Yanguang, courtesy name Xiuzhi, was a man of Wushi in Anding.
Liang Yanguang, courtesy name Xiuzhi, was a man of Wuzhi in Anding.
In the place name 烏氏 the character 氏 is read zhī (Wuzhi).
He answered: "If so, Huang Ba and Xi Sui are your guilty men."
He answered: "If so, Huang Ba and Gong Sui are your guilty men."
襲遂 paired with Huang Ba is the Han model official Gong Sui (龔遂); 襲 is a graphic variant/error for 龔.
He answered: "If so, Huang Ba and Xi Sui are your guilty men."
He answered: "If so, Huang Ba and Gong Sui are your guilty men."
襲遂 paired with Huang Ba is the Han model official Gong Sui (龔遂).
Those who studied diligently with unusual ability and whose clever orders were heard of—he set a feast in the hall; the rest all sat beneath the corridor.
Those who studied diligently with outstanding ability and were known for intelligence and excellence he seated in the hall and set out a feast for; the rest all sat beneath the corridor.
聰令有聞 means intelligent, excellent and well reputed; 令 here is "fine/excellent", not "orders".
Yanguang brought him to the school to view the image of Han Boyu weeping before his mother.

Yanguang did not punish him, but took him to the provincial school and had him view, in the Confucius temple, the image of Han Boyu weeping before his mother because her beating no longer hurt as her strength had failed.
The idiomatic line omits 弗之罪 (he did not punish him), the Confucius temple (孔子廟), and the reason for Han Boyu's grief.
He died in office; posthumously enfeoffed over four provinces, posthumous title Xiang.
He died in office and was posthumously granted the post of Inspector of the four provinces of Ji, Ding, Ying and Qing; his posthumous name was Xiang.
贈…刺史 is a posthumous grant of an inspectorship, not an enfeoffment; the four provinces are named in the source.
He died in office; posthumously enfeoffed as Governor of Ji, Ding, Ying, and Qing Provinces, posthumous title Xiang.
He died in office; he was posthumously granted Governor of the four provinces Ji, Ding, Ying, and Qing; his posthumous name was Xiang.
贈 is a posthumous grant of office; "enfeoffed" wrongly implies a fief.
As a pillar's son he was appointed palace guard of the fifth order.
As the heir of a Supreme Pillar of State, he was by precedent granted the rank of Yitong (Equal in Honor).
上柱國世子 is the heir of a Supreme Pillar of State; 儀同 is the honorary rank Equal in Honor, not a "palace guard of the fifth order".
As son of a supreme pillar of state, by precedent he was appointed Palace Guard of the Fifth Order.
As heir of a Supreme Pillar of State, by precedent he was granted Yitong (Equal in Honor).
儀同 is the rank Equal in Honor [to the Three Excellencies], not "Palace Guard of the Fifth Order"; 世子 is heir.
In the Liaodong campaign he led martial guard troops as deputy on the Lulong route.
In the Liaodong campaign he served as Martial Guard General and as deputy of the Lulong Route army.
領武賁郎將 means he held the post of Martial Guard General; he did not "lead martial guard troops".
In the Liaodong campaign he led Martial Guard General and served as deputy on the Lulong route.
In the Liaodong campaign he held the post of Martial Guard General and served as deputy of the Lulong Route army.
領 here means to hold the office concurrently; "led Martial Guard General" is ungrammatical and wrong.
When Yang Xuangan rebelled, his brother Xuanzong fled before news arrived; Wenqian did not notice.
When Yang Xuangan rebelled, his younger brother Xuanzong, a Martial Guard General, had been serving under Wenqian; before word of Xuangan's revolt arrived Xuanzong fled, and Wenqian did not notice.
The idiomatic line omits that Xuanzong had been placed under Wenqian (先隸文謙), which explains Wenqian's punishment, and his office.
His father Guan served Wei and was executed by the Gao clan.
His father Guan served Wei as Inspector of Southern Yanzhou and Marquis of Heyang, and was executed by the Gao clan.
The idiomatic line omits the offices 南兗州刺史 and the title 河陽侯.
When Yuwen Hu held power, he was made chief jailer.
When Grand Steward Yuwen Hu held power, he appointed Shulüe Commandant.
中尉 is the Commandant (a guard/police command), not a "chief jailer"; the title 大塚宰 (Grand Steward) is omitted.
When Grand Minister Yuwen Hu held power, he was made chief jailer.
When Grand Steward Yuwen Hu held power, he brought him in as Commandant.
中尉 is the Commandant, not "chief jailer".
In Yuwen Jiong's rebellion he guarded Daliang and was made grand general.
In Yuchi Jiong's rebellion he guarded Daliang; for military merit he was made Grand General and again Inspector of Bianzhou.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not "Yuwen Jiong"; the reappointment to Bianzhou (復為汴州刺史) was omitted.
In Yuwen Jiong's rebellion he guarded Daliang; for military merit he was made Grand General and again Administrator of Bianzhou.
In Yuchi Jiong's rebellion he guarded Daliang; for military merit he was made Grand General and again Administrator of Bianzhou.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong; the surname 尉遲 is not Yuwen.
When Wen took the throne, he was advanced to upper grand general and duke of Anding.
When Emperor Wen of Sui took the throne, he was advanced to Upper Grand General and promoted to Duke of Anding Commandery.
"Wen" alone is unclear; 隋文帝 is Emperor Wen of Sui, and 安定郡公 is a commandery-level dukedom.
Though without learning, he had grounds to rely on; yet following his own mind alone, he darkly accorded with principle.
Though he had no learning to rely on, yet following his own mind and independent views, he tacitly accorded with principle.
雖無學術有所依據 means he lacked learning on which to base himself; the literal line reverses this into "he had grounds to rely on".
Posthumously enfeoffed as governor of Bo, posthumous title Xiang.
He was posthumously granted the post of Inspector of Bozhou, and his posthumous name was Xiang.
贈亳州刺史 is a posthumous grant of office, not an enfeoffment.
Posthumously enfeoffed as Governor of Bo Province, posthumous title Xiang.
He was posthumously granted Governor of Bo Province; his posthumous name was Xiang.
贈 is a posthumous grant of office, not enfeoffment.
In Wei he was recommended as filial and incorrupt and ranked first in the archery examination.
In Wei he was recommended as filial and incorrupt and placed in the first class of the policy-question examination.
射策 is the examination in which candidates answer drawn policy questions, not an archery examination.
In Wei he was examined as Filial and Incorrupt and in archery examination ranked first class.
In Wei he was selected as Filial and Incorrupt and in the policy-question examination ranked first class.
射策 is answering drawn written questions, not archery.
In the founding of Kaihuang he was summoned and appointed Administrator of Runan.
Early in Kaihuang he was summoned and appointed Administrator of Runan.
開皇初 means early in the Kaihuang era; "In the founding of Kaihuang" is ungrammatical and misleading.
The emperor praised him, advanced him to upper palace guard of the third order, and made him governor of Yi.
The emperor was delighted, praised him by edict, and advanced him to Upper Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies and Inspector of Yi Province.
上儀同三司 is the rank Upper Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies, not a "palace guard of the third order"; 下詔褒美 is an edict of praise.
The emperor was very pleased, issued an edict praising him, and advanced him to Upper Palace Guard of the Third Order and Governor of Yi Province.
The emperor was very pleased, issued an edict praising him, and advanced him to Upper Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies and Governor of Yi Province.
上儀同三司 is a rank title, not "Upper Palace Guard of the Third Order".
He retired on an gracious imperial edict.
Later he asked to retire, and the emperor graciously granted it by edict.
"on an gracious" is ungrammatical, and the line omits that he requested retirement (請致仕) and that the emperor assented (聽之).
In Renshou Duke Yang Ji saw Jingmao's vigor undiminished and reported it.
In the Renshou era, Yang Ji, Duke of Shangming, went on a mission to Hebei, saw that Jingmao's vigor was undiminished, and reported it on his return.
The idiomatic line omits the title 上明公 and the Hebei mission.
Gongyi was orphaned young and raised by his mother’s family, who personally taught him the Documents and the commentaries.
Gongyi was orphaned young and raised by his mother, who personally taught him the Documents and the commentaries.
母氏 conventionally denotes the mother herself; rendering it as "his mother's family" changes the referent.
Gongyi was orphaned early and was raised by his mother’s family; they personally taught him the Documents and the Commentaries.
Gongyi was orphaned early and was raised by his mother; she personally taught him the Documents and the Commentaries.
He therefore sent out officials to patrol within the prefecture; wherever there was illness they were brought on beds and litters to the investigation hall.
He therefore sent out officials to patrol within the prefecture; wherever there was illness they were brought on beds and litters and placed in the office hall.
査事 (廳事) is the government office hall, not an "investigation hall"; 安置 (placed) is omitted.
He told kin: "Life and death are fate; you abandoned the sick, so they died.
Then he summoned their kin and told them: "Life and death are decided by fate and have nothing to do with contact; before, you abandoned them, and that is why they died.
The idiomatic line omits 不關相著 (not caused by contact), the core of his argument.
On taking office he first went to the prison, exposed the jail and sat beside it, personally examining and questioning.
On taking office he first went to the prison, sat in the open beside the cells, and personally examined and questioned the prisoners.
露坐牢側 means he sat in the open beside the jail; "exposed the jail" misreads 露.
Most litigants yielded twice and stopped.
Most litigants both yielded and stopped.
兩讓 means both parties yielded, not that they "yielded twice".
Yellow silver from the mountains was offered; prayers brought sounds of music in the air.

The mountains produced yellow silver, which he obtained and presented; an edict sent Lou Ze, Gentleman of the Waterworks Bureau, to pray at Gongyi's place, and the sound of metal, stone, silk and bamboo instruments was heard in the air.
The idiomatic line omits the edict, the envoy 婁崱 and the place of prayer.

The mountains produced yellow silver; he obtained it and presented it; an edict sent Master of Waterworks Lou Kai to pray at Gongyi's place, and there was heard in the air the sound of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo.

The mountains produced yellow silver; he obtained and presented it; an edict sent Gentleman of the Waterworks Bureau Lou Ze to pray at Gongyi's place, and there was heard in the air the sound of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo.
崱 is read zè (Lou Ze), not Kai; 水部郎 is a Gentleman of the Waterworks Bureau.
When Wen took the throne he became vice minister of waterworks and baron of Shuaidao.
When Emperor Wen of Sui took the throne, he was promoted to Vice Minister of Waterworks and enfeoffed as Earl of Shuaidao County.
縣伯 is a county earl, not a baron; "Wen" alone is unclear for 隋文帝.
When Emperor Wen of Sui received the abdication he was promoted to Vice Minister of Waterworks and enfeoffed Baron of Shuaidao.
When Emperor Wen of Sui received the abdication he was promoted to Vice Minister of Waterworks and enfeoffed Earl of Shuaidao County.
The emperor asked Wei and Hong, "Among them, who has the purest name in the realm?"
The emperor asked Nayan Su Wei and Minister of Personnel Niu Hong: "Among them, who has the purest name in the realm?"
The idiomatic line reduces the named ministers to "Wei and Hong" and drops their offices.
The emperor said to Master of Documents Su Wei and Minister of Personnel Niu Hong: "Among them, who has the foremost pure name in the realm?"
The emperor said to Nayan (head of the Chancellery) Su Wei and Minister of Personnel Niu Hong: "Among them, who has the foremost pure name in the realm?"
納言 is the head of the Chancellery under Sui, not "Master of Documents".
He rose from secretariat clerk to palace guard through military merit, serving ably in several provinces.

He began as a clerk of the Department of State Affairs, was later granted the rank of Yitong (Equal in Honor) for military merit, and served ably as marshal and chief administrator of several provinces.
儀同 is the rank Equal in Honor, not "palace guard"; 司馬、長史 are specific provincial posts.

At first he was a clerk in the Secretariat of the Master of Documents; later for military merit he was made Palace Guard of the Same Order, and served successively as marshal and chief administrator of several provinces—all with reputations for ability.

At first he was a clerk in the Department of State Affairs; later for military merit he was made Yitong (Equal in Honor), and served successively as marshal and chief administrator of several provinces—all with reputations for ability.
儀同 is the rank Equal in Honor, not "Palace Guard of the Same Order".
Jing Su, courtesy name Jingjian, was from Puzhou in Hedong.
Jing Su, courtesy name Jingjian, was from Puban in Hedong.
蒲阪 is Puban, not Puzhou.
Jing Su, styled Jingjian, was a man of Puzhou in Hedong.
Jing Su, styled Jingjian, was a man of Puban in Hedong.
蒲阪 is Puban, not Puzhou.
In the founding of Kaihuang he was Magistrate of Anling, with a reputation for ability.
Early in Kaihuang he was Magistrate of Anling, with a reputation for ability.
開皇初 means early in Kaihuang; "In the founding of Kaihuang" is ungrammatical.
In the founding of Kaihuang he was Magistrate of Pingxiang, going to office alone on horseback.
Early in Kaihuang he was Magistrate of Pingxiang, going to office alone on horseback.
開皇初 means early in Kaihuang; "In the founding of Kaihuang" is ungrammatical.
When people had disputes and lawsuits he would calmly explain with principle and righteousness, not adding punishment by whip; each withdrew blaming himself.
When people had disputes and lawsuits he would patiently explain principle and righteousness to them, without prosecution or punishment; each withdrew blaming himself.
不加繩劾 means without binding or prosecuting; "punishment by whip" is invented.
Left Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Gao Jiong reported his conduct; the emperor summoned him.
Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Gao Jiong reported his conduct; the emperor summoned him.
尚書左僕射 is the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, not of the "Imperial Secretariat".
He began as a mourning officer, served as clerk in Fengyi and Wuyang, and became chief of Guixiang.

Deshen began as a pallbearer at the funeral of Emperor Wen of Sui, later served as clerk of Fengyi Commandery and as household officer and clerk of Wuyang Commandery, and for his ability became chief of Guixiang.
The idiomatic line omits that he was 挽郎 for Emperor Wen of Sui and the posts 司戶 and 書佐.

Deshen at first was a mourning officer for Emperor Wen of Sui; later he served successively as clerk of Fengyi Commandery and as household and clerk of Wuyang Commandery; for ability he was transferred to Chief of Guixiang.

Deshen at first was a pallbearer for Emperor Wen of Sui; later he served successively as Clerk of Fengyi Commandery and as Household Officer and Clerk of Wuyang Commandery; for ability he was transferred to Chief of Guixiang.
司戶 is the Household Officer; "household and clerk" is garbled.
Vice Administrator Baocang lost battles and repeatedly levied the people under military law.

Vice Administrator Yuan Baocang, ordered by edict to hunt down bandits, lost battle after battle; whenever his weapons ran out he levied them from the people, always enforcing military law, and this happened several times.
The idiomatic line drops the surname 元, the edict to pursue bandits, and the exhaustion of weapons that caused the levies.
Neighboring cities' construction all gathered at the investigation hall; officials and people supervised one another; day and night noisy; still they could not finish.
Neighboring cities' construction was all gathered in the office halls; officials and people urged one another on, noisy day and night, yet still could not finish.
査事 (廳事) is the government office hall, not an "investigation hall".
Commissioners ruled for Guixiang after both counties sued.
When the commissioners bearing credentials, Wei Ji, Du Zheng and others, arrived, both counties brought their suit before them, and they ruled for Guixiang.
The idiomatic line omits the named commissioners 韋霽 and 杜整.
Someone said to them: "Li Mi's troops are near Jincheng, twenty-odd li from here; if you must return, who can forbid you? Why torment yourselves so!
Someone said to them: "Li Mi's troops are near Jinyong, twenty-odd li from here; if you must return, who can forbid you?
金墉 is Jinyong (the Jinyong fortress), not Jincheng; the final sentence belongs to s0583.
